preamble.summary: Chapter 30 treats three major themes in sequence: the discipline of children (vv. 1-13), the supreme value of health (vv. 14-20), and the importance of cheerfulness and the danger of sorrow (vv. 21-27). Ben Sira advocates firm discipline of sons, argues that good health surpasses all wealth, and concludes with a memorable exhortation not to surrender one's heart to grief.
preamble.remarkable: The section on child-rearing is among the most forceful in ancient literature, advocating corporal discipline with an intensity that reflects the ancient conviction that an undisciplined child is a disgrace worse than death. The health section contains the striking declaration 'No wealth is better than health of body, and no gladness above the joy of the heart' (v. 16) -- a proto-holistic view of wellbeing that values physical and emotional health above material prosperity. The closing injunction to 'drive away grief far from you' (v. 23) recognizes sorrow as a destructive force that can be actively resisted.
preamble.friction: The advocacy of corporal punishment (vv. 1-13) is the most problematic aspect of this chapter for modern readers. The language -- 'beat his sides,' 'bow down his neck in youth' -- reflects pedagogical assumptions that are now widely rejected. The absolute equation of health with happiness also oversimplifies the experiences of those living with chronic illness or disability.
preamble.connections: Proverbs 13:24 (spare the rod, spoil the child); Proverbs 23:13-14 (do not withhold discipline); Proverbs 17:22 (a cheerful heart is good medicine); Philippians 4:4 (rejoice in the Lord always); Ecclesiastes 11:10 (remove vexation from your heart).

verses.text_latin: Qui diligit filium suum adsiduat illi flagella ut laetetur in novissimo suo.
verses.rendering: Whoever loves his son applies the rod to him continually, so that he may rejoice in the end.
translator_notes: The paradox of parental love expressed through discipline: the rod now produces joy later.

key_terms.note: Flagella (whips/rods) -- the instrument of discipline is named frankly. The ancient assumption is that physical correction is an expression of parental love, not cruelty.

verses.text_latin: Qui docet filium suum laudabitur in illo et in medio domesticorum in illo gloriabitur.
verses.rendering: Whoever instructs his son will be praised because of him, and in the midst of his household he will glory in him.

verses.text_latin: Qui docet filium suum in zelum mittit inimicum et in medio amicorum gloriabitur in illo.
verses.rendering: Whoever teaches his son provokes his enemy to jealousy, and before friends he will glory in him.

verses.text_latin: Mortuus est pater illius et quasi non est mortuus similem enim reliquit sibi post se.
verses.rendering: His father has died, and yet it is as though he has not died, for he has left behind one like himself.
translator_notes: The well-raised son is a form of immortality -- the father lives on in his character.

verses.text_latin: In vita sua vidit et laetatus est in illo et in obitu suo non est contristatus nec confusus est coram inimicis.
verses.rendering: In his lifetime he looked on him and was glad, and in his death he was not grieved, nor was he ashamed before his enemies.

verses.text_latin: Reliquit enim defensorem domus contra inimicos et amicis reddentem gratiam.
verses.rendering: For he left behind a defender of the house against enemies, and one who repays kindness to friends.

verses.text_latin: Pro animabus filiorum conligabit vulnera sua et super omnem vocem turbabuntur viscera eius.
verses.rendering: For the souls of his children he will bind up his wounds, and at every cry his heart will be troubled.
translator_notes: The tender side of the disciplinarian: the father who punishes also suffers -- every wound on the child is felt in the parent's heart.

verses.text_latin: Equus indomitus evadit durus et filius remissus evadet praeceps.
verses.rendering: An untamed horse becomes stubborn, and an unchecked son becomes headstrong.

verses.text_latin: Lacta filium et paventem te faciet lude cum eo et contristabit te.
verses.rendering: Pamper your son and he will terrify you; play with him and he will grieve you.

verses.text_latin: Non conrideas illi ne condoleas et in novissimo obstupescent dentes tui.
verses.rendering: Do not laugh with him, lest you share his pain, and in the end your teeth will be set on edge.

verses.text_latin: Non des illi potestatem in iuventute et ne despicias cogitatus illius.
verses.rendering: Do not give him authority in his youth, and do not overlook his errors.

verses.text_latin: Curva cervicem eius in iuventute et tunde latera eius dum infans est ne forte induret et non credat tibi et erit tibi dolor animae.
verses.rendering: Bow down his neck in youth, and beat his sides while he is a child, lest he become stubborn and disobey you, and there will be grief for your soul.

verses.text_latin: Doce filium tuum et operare in illo ne in turpitudinem illius offendas.
verses.rendering: Teach your son and work with him, lest you stumble through his shameful behavior.

verses.text_latin: Melior est pauper sanus et fortis viribus quam dives inbecillis et flagellatus malitia.
verses.rendering: Better is a poor person who is healthy and strong in body than a rich man who is feeble and afflicted with disease.
translator_notes: The pivot to the health section: physical wellbeing outranks material wealth.

verses.text_latin: Salus animae in sanctitate iustitiae melior est omni auro et argento et corpus validum super censum inmmensum.
verses.rendering: Health of soul in holiness and justice is better than all gold and silver, and a strong body is above immense wealth.

verses.text_latin: Non est census super censum salutis corporis et non est oblectamentum super cordis gaudium.
verses.rendering: No wealth is better than health of body, and no gladness is above the joy of the heart.
translator_notes: The chapter's most quotable verse -- a holistic vision of human flourishing that integrates body and spirit.

key_terms.note: Inner joy, not external pleasure -- the heart's own delight, which is independent of circumstances.

verses.text_latin: Melior est mors quam vita amara et requies aeterna quam languor perseverans.
verses.rendering: Better is death than a bitter life, and eternal rest than chronic illness.
translator_notes: A stark declaration: unrelenting suffering can make death preferable. Ben Sira acknowledges suffering's capacity to overwhelm.

verses.text_latin: Bona absconsa in ore clauso quasi adpositiones epularum circumpositi sepulchro.
verses.rendering: Good things poured out upon a mouth that is closed are like offerings of food placed around a tomb.
translator_notes: Wasted gifts: food for the dead benefits no one. Health unused or joy unexpressed is equally futile.

verses.text_latin: Quid proderit libatio idolo nec enim manducabit nec odorabitur sic qui effugatur a Domino.
verses.rendering: What good is an offering to an idol? For it can neither eat nor smell. So is the one who is driven away by the Lord.

verses.text_latin: Portans mercedem iniquitatis qui videt oculis et ingemescit sicut spado conplectens virginem et suspirans.
verses.rendering: Like one bearing the wages of iniquity is he who sees with his eyes and groans, like a eunuch embracing a young woman and sighing.
translator_notes: The eunuch simile returns from 20:4 -- desire without capacity for fulfillment is the image of frustration itself.

verses.text_latin: Tristitiam non des animae tuae et non adfligas temet ipsum in consilio tuo.
verses.rendering: Do not give your soul over to sorrow, and do not afflict yourself by your own counsel.
translator_notes: The turn to emotional self-care: sorrow is presented as something one can refuse to cultivate.

verses.text_latin: Iucunditas cordis haec est vita hominis et thesaurus sine defectione sanctitatis et exultatio viri est longaevitas.
verses.rendering: Gladness of heart -- this is the life of a person, and an unfailing treasure of holiness; and the exultation of a man is length of days.

verses.text_latin: Miserere animae tuae placens Deo et contine et congrega cor tuum in sanctitate eius et tristitiam longe repelle a te.
verses.rendering: Have mercy on your own soul by pleasing God; and restrain yourself, and gather your heart in his holiness, and drive sorrow far away from you.
translator_notes: Self-mercy through God-pleasing: the healthiest thing one can do for one's soul is to align with God and expel grief.

verses.text_latin: Multos enim occidit tristitia et non est utilitas in illa.
verses.rendering: For sorrow has killed many, and there is no profit in it.
translator_notes: A blunt medical observation: grief kills. The ancients recognized what modern medicine confirms about the physiological effects of prolonged sorrow.

verses.text_latin: Zelus et iracundia minuent dies et ante tempus senectam adducet cogitatus.
verses.rendering: Jealousy and anger shorten one's days, and anxiety brings old age before its time.

verses.text_latin: Splendidum cor et bonum in epulis est epulae enim illius diligenter fiunt.
verses.rendering: A cheerful and good heart will feast continually, for his banquets are prepared with care.

verses.text_latin: Vigilia honestatis tabefaciet carnes et cogitatus illius auferet somnum.
verses.rendering: Sleepless anxiety over possessions wastes the flesh, and worry about them drives away sleep.
translator_notes: The chapter ends on a warning: wealth that produces anxiety destroys the health it was supposed to secure.
